wikispec.title: Generation specs
wikispec.about.power: Peak output of this engine in kilowatts, with metric horsepower in brackets (converted). Some tables give a range, for example before and after a facelift or for different markets.
wikispec.about.displacement: Engine size in litres, as the manufacturer names it (a "2.4" is really about 2,393 cm³). Bigger usually means more torque and more fuel burned.
wikispec.about.fuel: What the engine runs on: petrol, diesel, electric, hybrid or LPG. A hybrid row combines a combustion engine with an electric motor.
wikispec.about.cylinders: Number of cylinders, when the source lists it. More cylinders usually run smoother and cost more to service.
wikispec.about.engineCode: The manufacturer’s code of the engine itself (for example T24A-FTS or 2TR-FE). Use it to find the right parts, oil or service data. Guessed from the code’s shape, as the source table does not label it.
wikispec.about.chassisCode: Internal code of the body / model version this engine was fitted to (for example TJA250 or FK1). Dealers and parts catalogues use it, and it may be on the car’s VIN plate. Guessed from the code’s shape.
wikispec.about.note: The body style, trim or market this engine row applies to (for example "Hybrid Sedan" or "Europe"). A car of the same generation in another market may have a different engine.
wikispec.about.years: Production years of this engine inside the generation, when the source gives them.
wikispec.about.raw: The row exactly as written in the Wikipedia table: no figure in it could be read unambiguously, so nothing was converted.
wikispec.about.layout: Which wheels the engine drives (front, rear, all-wheel) and where the engine sits. Several layouts separated by ";" mean different versions offer different drives.
wikispec.about.transmission: Gearbox types offered in this generation (manual, automatic, CVT, dual-clutch).
wikispec.about.wheelbaseMm: Distance between the front and rear axles. A longer wheelbase usually means more rear legroom and a smoother ride.
wikispec.about.lengthMm: Overall length of the car, bumper to bumper.
wikispec.about.widthMm: Overall width of the body, usually without the mirrors.
wikispec.about.heightMm: Overall height of the empty car; roof rails or an antenna can add a little.
wikispec.about.kerbKg: Weight of the car ready to drive, without driver and cargo (kerb weight). Versions differ by 100 kg or more depending on engine and trim.
wikispec.about.fuelTankL: Fuel tank volume in litres. With the consumption figure it gives a rough range on one tank.
wikispec.hint.engines: One card per engine offered in this generation. Tap ❓ on a row to see what it means.
wikispec.hint.drive: How the power reaches the road and which gearboxes this generation offers.
wikispec.hint.dimensions: Catalogue figures of the body. Shown only because the Dutch register has none for this model.

wikispec.info.match: The engine that fits this car’s registered fuel, displacement (±3 %) and power (±7 %) is highlighted and listed first; for the others the brackets show how they differ. Registry figures are rounded and some are missing, so treat it as a best guess.
wikispec.about.enginePosition: Where the engine sits in the car. Front is the most common; a rear or middle engine is typical of sports cars and some small cars.
wikispec.about.drivenWheels: Which wheels receive the power. Several values mean different versions of the generation offer different drives; the source does not say which one this car has.
wikispec.about.gearbox.manual: Gearbox shifted by the driver with a clutch pedal. The number is how many gears it has; several numbers mean different versions.
wikispec.about.gearbox.automatic: Classic torque-converter automatic that shifts by itself. The number is how many gears it has.
wikispec.about.gearbox.dct: Dual-clutch gearbox (DSG, PDK, PowerShift and similar): two clutches shift very fast without the driver pressing a pedal.
wikispec.about.gearbox.cvt: Continuously variable transmission: no fixed gears, so the engine stays at its best speed. Hybrids use an electronic version (eCVT).
wikispec.about.gearbox.amt: A manual gearbox shifted by a computer (robotised or semi-automatic). Cheaper than an automatic, but shifts can feel slower.
wikispec.about.gearbox.single: One fixed ratio, as in electric cars: no gear changes at all.

size.title: Size & parking
section.about.size:
One place for how big this car is and where it fits.
Figures - length, width, height and wheelbase are merged from the best source: RDW (Dutch register, fleet median), then the Wikipedia article of its generation, then the VIN decode
Forecast - a missing figure is estimated from the others and the body shape; it is dashed, marked ≈ and never presented as data
Class - an approximate European segment (A–F, SUV, MPV) by length, not an official class
Parking and garage - the car drawn in Ukrainian, German and US parking places and in typical garages, with a verdict
Norms - the rules behind the numbers, with links to the sources ↗
These are catalogue and fleet values for the model, not measured on this car; the width does not include the mirrors
size.typicalOnly: No published dimensions for this model - the typical {{shape}} is shown (our forecast, not data).
size.estimatedNote: Values marked ≈ are our forecast from the other figures and the body shape, not data.
size.tab.schema.intro: The car drawn to scale from the figures below, side and top view, front to the right. Dashed arrows are forecast figures.
size.tab.parking.intro: The car in the parking places of Ukraine, Germany and the USA, drawn at one scale. The verdict counts the mirrors (+20 cm) and room to open the doors.
size.tab.garage.intro: The car in a typical single box and a double garage, seen from above: free space around it, the door and the lintel height, plus tips on where parking is easy or hard.

size.shape.label: Body shape
size.class.label: Size class
size.about.lengthMm: Overall length, bumper to bumper, in millimetres (metres in brackets). It decides the parking-place length, the class and the gap you need to park parallel.
size.about.widthMm: Overall width of the body without the mirrors. Mirrors add about 20 cm; the fit verdicts count them.
size.about.heightMm: Overall height from the road to the roof, without roof rails or a roof box (a box adds about 40 cm). It decides garage doors, underground car parks and mechanical parking lifts.
size.about.wheelbaseMm: Distance between the centres of the front and rear axles. A longer wheelbase usually means more rear legroom and a wider turning circle; it also sets where the wheels are drawn.
size.about.shape: The outline used for the drawing: the registry body of this car first, else the model’s usual body in the Dutch register, else the VIN decode. “Passenger car” is a generic outline used when no source names the body.
size.about.class:
An approximate European segment worked out from the length and body shape. It is a rule of thumb for orientation, not an official or manufacturer’s class.
A - mini, under 3.8 m
B - small
C - compact (Golf class)
D - mid-size / large family
E - executive
F - luxury, over 5.1 m
SUV / crossover - its own segment with a size word: small, compact, mid-size, large
MPV / minivan - its own segment with the same size words
Van - a van-type body (panel van, minibus, people carrier on a van base); no length classes
Pickup - a body with an open cargo bed; no length classes
Motorcycles, buses and trucks have no class
size.about.estimate: A forecast: a missing figure is derived from the known ones and the typical proportions of this body shape (a car 10 % longer is about 5 % wider and 3 % taller). It can be several centimetres off. Verdicts built on forecast figures say so.
size.schema.alt: Side and top view of {{name}}: length {{length}}, width {{width}}, height {{height}}
size.schema.caption: Drawn to scale from the figures below; the wheels sit at the wheelbase. Dashed arrows are forecast figures.
size.verdict.about.comfortable: Enough room to park and open the doors without effort: at least 40 cm free across a place (mirrors counted) and 20 cm along it; at a garage door 30 cm of clearance and 15 cm under the lintel.
size.verdict.about.tight: It fits, but expect to fold the mirrors, park carefully and squeeze out of the door: less than the comfortable margins above, but not negative.
size.verdict.about.no: The car is wider, longer or taller than the place: it will stick out or scrape.
size.bay.about.ua: ДБН В.2.3-15:2007, clause 5.2: the place for a medium car on a storage car park is 2.5 × 5.3 m. It already includes a safety gap of at least 0.5 m (which may be raised to 0.7 m).
size.bay.about.uaTemp: The same clause of ДБН В.2.3-15:2007 allows 2.3 × 5.0 m on temporary car parks.
size.bay.about.de: Garagenverordnung of the German states (Saxony § 4 as the example): a place is at least 5 m long and 2.30 m wide with no wall beside it; 2.40 m with a wall on one side, 2.50 m between two walls, 3.50 m for disabled drivers. The 2.30 m minimum is shown. State law: check your state’s current text.
size.bay.about.us: The usual US city-code stall is 9 × 18 ft (2.74 × 5.49 m); many cities accept 8.5 ft wide spaces. There is no national norm: this is an example from one city code.
size.bay.alt: The car inside the parking place “{{name}}”
size.bay.margin: Free: {{side}} cm each side, {{length}} cm along the car.
size.mirrors: Mirrors are counted as +20 cm of width (they are in no dataset) and the doors need room beside the car. An estimate for orientation, not a legal test.
size.garage.about.single: A typical Ukrainian garage-cooperative box: 3 × 6 m inside, a door about 2.4 m wide and 2.1 m high. These are typical sizes, not a norm: measure yours.
size.garage.about.double: Two cars side by side in 6 × 6 m, with a 4.8 m door (2.4 m per car). Typical sizes, not a norm.
size.garage.width: Free width: {{n}} cm in each gap (walls and cars).
size.garage.length: Free length: {{n}} cm beyond the car.
size.garage.door: Door clearance: {{n}} cm beside the car (mirrors counted).
size.garage.alt: The car inside the “{{name}}”, seen from above
size.garage.typical: Garage sizes are typical values, not a norm: measure your own door and box. Mirrors are counted as +20 cm.
size.tips.title: Where it is easy, where it is hard
size.tip.tiny.title: Easy almost everywhere: at {{length}} m it slips into short bays and tight courtyards.
size.tip.tiny.about: Cars under 3.8 m are easy to park across, along and in short gaps; in a courtyard two of them can often use the room of one large car.
size.tip.long.title: Long ({{length}} m): hard to turn in tight courtyards and short bays.
size.tip.long.about: From about 4.9 m the car is as long as the 5.0–5.3 m bays leave room for; allow a wide approach to reverse in.
size.tip.wide.title: Wide ({{width}} m with mirrors): narrow gates and bays are tight.
size.tip.wide.about: A wide car leaves little room to open doors in a 2.3–2.5 m place and may not pass old courtyard arches. Fold the mirrors and choose end places.
size.tip.parallel.title: Parallel parking needs a gap of about {{gap}} m.
size.tip.parallel.about: The car plus about a metre to swing in. With less you will need several attempts.
size.tip.mechanical.title: Taller than most mechanical parking lifts ({{height}} m > {{limit}} m).
size.tip.mechanical.about: Puzzle and stack parking systems usually allow about 1.55 m of height; this car may not fit them. Check the plate on the system.
size.tip.roofBox.title: Near the underground clearance: with a roof box it is {{withBox}} m.
size.tip.roofBox.about: Underground car parks usually post about 2.0 m. A roof box adds about 40 cm, so take it off before driving in.
size.tip.clearanceNo.title: Taller than a typical underground clearance ({{height}} m > {{limit}} m).
size.tip.clearanceNo.about: Underground car parks and many garage doors stop at about 2.0 m. Look for the height sign before you drive in.
size.tip.moto.title: Easy: a motorcycle takes a fraction of a car place.
size.tip.moto.about: ДБН В.2.3-15:2007 plans a place of 2.4 × 0.8 m for a solo motorcycle (2.4 × 1.7 m with a sidecar).
size.norms.roadIntro: A vehicle above these sizes is oversize and needs a special permit to drive. Ordinary cars are far below them; vans, trucks and buses may not be.
size.norms.classesNote: Approximate segments by length; SUVs and MPVs are listed by their own segment and a size word. Not an official classification.
size.road.about.width: ПДР clause 22.5(а): a vehicle wider than 2.6 m is oversize. Agricultural machinery has wider limits outside built-up areas.
size.road.about.height: ПДР clause 22.5(а): a vehicle higher than 4.0 m from the road is oversize (4.35 m for container carriers on approved routes).
size.road.about.length: ПДР clause 22.5(а): a single lorry or bus longer than 12 m is oversize.
size.road.trains: A tractor with a semi-trailer may be up to {{tractor}} m, a lorry with a trailer up to {{train}} m; a load may extend up to 2 m behind.
size.link.ua-dbn.title: ДБН В.2.3-15:2007 “Car parks and garages for passenger cars”
size.link.ua-dbn.what: ДБН В.2.3-15:2007 is the Ukrainian state building norm (ДБН) “Car parks and garages for passenger cars”: it sets how parking places, ramps and garages must be designed. Clause 5.2 gives the size of a place (2.5 × 5.3 m); clause 4.6 sets the design car (up to 6 m long and 2.1 m wide). Amendments no. 1–3.
size.link.ua-pdr.title: ПДР України (КМУ № 1306), clause 22.5
size.link.ua-pdr.what: The Ukrainian Road Traffic Rules (Cabinet of Ministers resolution of 10.10.2001 no. 1306). Clause 22.5(а) lists the maximum permitted dimensions of a vehicle: width 2.6 m, height 4.0 m and lengths by vehicle type.
size.link.de-gav.title: Garagenverordnung (Saxony), § 4 Einstellplätze und Fahrgassen
size.link.de-gav.what: German parking-place rules are state law (Länder); Saxony’s garage regulation is shown as an example. Check the current version for your state.
size.link.us-stall.title: Example US city code: 9 × 18 ft stall (Lindon, Utah)
size.link.us-stall.what: There is no US national parking-stall norm; each city sets its own. Lindon’s code is shown as an example of the common 9 × 18 ft stall.

read.fleet.colorFacts.title: Colours in the registry: what to know
read.fleet.colorFacts.palette.title: Only 11 base colours
read.fleet.colorFacts.palette.text: Ukrainian MIA service centres register one of 11 colours: black, blue, green, beige, red, violet, orange, yellow, white, brown and grey. There is no pink or turquoise entry, so a pink car is recorded under another base colour or as "combined".
read.fleet.colorFacts.shade.title: A shade change is not a reason to re-register
read.fleet.colorFacts.shade.text: A red car that became dark red is still red, so there is no need to visit a service centre. A white car that became pink is a real colour change.
read.fleet.colorFacts.multi.title: Several colours on one body
read.fleet.colorFacts.multi.text: The main colour is that of the lower part of the body. The roof, bonnet or boot may be another colour while it covers no more than 50% of the area. If it covers more, the documents record a combined colour.
read.fleet.colorFacts.chameleon.title: "Chameleon" paint
read.fleet.colorFacts.chameleon.text: The finish changes colour with light and viewing angle. Its colour is established by an expert examination, and the registration certificate records the main, dominant colour.
read.fleet.colorFacts.wrap.title: A film over the original colour
read.fleet.colorFacts.wrap.text: A wrap is glued on top of the factory paint and does not alter the paint itself: after careful removal the paint stays underneath, if it was in good condition. A full wrap that changes the main colour is a reason to ask an MIA service centre about updating the registration. A partial wrap (roof, mirrors, bonnet, trim) that keeps the main colour is a different case. A film will not hide rust or peeling lacquer, and it comes off worse from them.
read.fleet.colorFacts.film.title: Vinyl, anti-gravel film and finishes
read.fleet.colorFacts.film.text: Vinyl changes the look: gloss, matt, satin, metallic, textured and decorative finishes. Anti-gravel (protective) film shields the lacquer from stones and scratches, and it is not the same thing. Matt vinyl should be washed without gloss-boosting products, and a pressure jet should not be held close to the film edges.
read.fleet.colorFacts.rules.title: Deadlines, fines and documents
read.fleet.colorFacts.rules.text: A car must be re-registered within 10 days of the colour change (clause 33 of the registration procedure, Cabinet resolution no. 1388) at any MIA service centre, with a passport or ID card and proof of residence (or a power of attorney). The owner gets a new certificate. A colour change alone is not grounds for a police stop, but the mismatch can be noticed during a document check. Article 121(6) of the Code of Administrative Offences carries an 850 UAH fine: a court upheld it for a Tesla Model S registered as blue but photographed green (case no. 932/3371/24, 2024).
read.fleet.colorFacts.data.title: What it means for the data
read.fleet.colorFacts.data.text: The colour in the registry is the one given at the last registration. A wrapped car often still shows its old colour while looking different in photos and on the road, so treat the colour in search as a guide, not a guarantee.

read.fleet.fuelFacts.title: Fuel: what to know
read.fleet.fuelFacts.trend.title: More fuel choice every year
read.fleet.fuelFacts.trend.text: For decades the fleet ran on petrol, diesel and gas (petrol + LPG is the classic Ukrainian conversion). That has changed: hybrids arrived, and after 2022 used electric cars flooded in, including ones long since dropped from the markets that built them. The registry therefore holds more and more fuel groups side by side, and the share of electric and hybrid cars is clearly higher among recent registrations. See the year chart above and the full fuel stats.
read.fleet.fuelFacts.history.title: A short history of fuel types
read.fleet.fuelFacts.history.text: Electric cars appeared in the 19th century and were among the most common at the start of the 20th. Karl Benz built his petrol car in 1886, Rudolf Diesel patented his engine in 1893, and the first series-built diesel passenger car (Mercedes-Benz 260 D) came in 1936. Autogas boomed in the 1930s-50s and returned during the oil crises. The Toyota Prius (1997) made the hybrid mainstream, the Tesla Roadster (2008) and Nissan Leaf (2010) did the same for electric cars, and the Hyundai ix35 FCEV (2013) and Toyota Mirai (2014) brought hydrogen.
read.fleet.fuelFacts.hybrids.title: Not all hybrids are the same
read.fleet.fuelFacts.hybrids.text: A mild hybrid with a 48 V system only assists the engine; a full hybrid (HEV) can drive on electricity but never plugs in; a plug-in hybrid (PHEV) has a larger battery and charges from the grid; a range-extender EV (REEV) drives on electricity while a petrol engine only recharges the battery. The registry usually records them as a combination, such as "petrol + electric".
read.fleet.fuelFacts.gas.title: Gas: LPG, methane and hydrogen
read.fleet.fuelFacts.gas.text: Autogas (LPG, propane-butane) is the most common conversion in Ukraine: gas equipment is fitted to a petrol car, so the registry shows a separate "petrol + gas" group. Methane (CNG) is stored compressed, and liquefied gas (LNG) is mostly for trucks. Hydrogen remains exotic, either in fuel cells or (rarely) a combustion engine.
read.fleet.fuelFacts.chargers.title: Charging connector types
read.fleet.fuelFacts.chargers.text: Type 1 (SAE J1772) is single-phase AC, typical of US and Japanese cars, around 7 kW. Type 2 (Mennekes) is the European AC standard, up to 22 kW. CCS (Combo) is the same inlet plus two DC pins for fast charging, up to 350 kW: CCS2 in Europe, CCS1 in the US. CHAdeMO is the Japanese fast-charging standard (Nissan Leaf), slowly being phased out. GB/T is the Chinese standard, separate for AC and DC. NACS (SAE J3400) is Tesla’s connector in North America; in Europe Tesla uses CCS2. Slow AC points give 3.7-22 kW, fast DC ones 50 to 350 kW and more. A car with a US inlet is charged in Ukraine through adapters.
read.fleet.fuelFacts.fuelQuality.title: Fuel quality: the EN 228 and EN 590 standards
read.fleet.fuelFacts.fuelQuality.text: The European standard EN 228 (petrol) sets 95 or 98 RON, at most 10 mg/kg of sulphur and limits on benzene (up to 1%) and aromatics. EN 590 (diesel) sets at most 10 mg/kg of sulphur, a cetane number of at least 51 and up to 7% biodiesel (FAME, grade B7). Ukraine applies the matching ДСТУ EN 228 and ДСТУ EN 590, and technical regulation no. 927 is aligned with EU Directive 98/70/EC; Euro-5 class fuel (by sulphur content) has been mandatory since 2016.
read.fleet.fuelFacts.e10.title: E10 petrol in Ukraine
read.fleet.fuelFacts.e10.text: From 1 July 2026 Ukrainian filling stations sell E10: up to 10% bioethanol in petrol, with the familiar grades (A-95 and so on). Market consultant Serhii Kuiun estimates it adds 50-70 kopecks per litre to the cost, under 1%. E10 is safe for modern cars; older ones may need minor fuel-system adjustments. If your car is old, a motorcycle or a classic, check the manufacturer’s manual. Source: RBC-Ukraine.
read.fleet.fuelFacts.labels.title: EU pump labels
read.fleet.fuelFacts.labels.text: EU pumps are labelled the same way everywhere: a circle for petrol (E5, E10), a square for diesel (B7) and a diamond for gas (CNG, LPG, hydrogen). The number is the bio-component: E10 is up to 10% ethanol, B7 up to 7% biodiesel. This comes from Directive 2014/94/EU (implementing regulation 2018/732).
read.fleet.fuelFacts.euro.title: Euro emission classes and the EU direction
read.fleet.fuelFacts.euro.text: Euro classes cap a car’s emissions: Euro 5 applies from 2009 and Euro 6 from 2014 (Regulation 715/2007). Regulation 2024/1257 (Euro 7) covers new vehicle types from 29 November 2026 and all new vehicles from November 2027, and for the first time limits brake and tyre emissions. The EU aims for zero CO₂ from new cars from 2035 (Regulation 2023/851); the rules are under review, so watch the news.
read.fleet.fuelFacts.chargingLaw.title: The EU charging law
read.fleet.fuelFacts.chargingLaw.text: The AFIR regulation (2023/1804) obliges EU states to build out charging: high-power DC points along the main corridors, payment by bank card with no registration and a common Type 2/CCS2 connector. That is why European cars carry CCS2 while American and Japanese ones need an adapter.
read.fleet.fuelFacts.data.title: What it means for the data
read.fleet.fuelFacts.data.text: Fuel in the registry is free text, so different spellings are folded onto the base fuels. Hybrids often appear as "petrol + electric", and a car converted to gas as "petrol + gas", even though its engine is formally petrol.

read.vin.anatomyIntro: Every car has a 17-character Vehicle Identification Number, and no two cars share one. Tap a part to see what it means, or type your own VIN.
read.vin.unknownMaker: We do not know this maker prefix, so the maker and country may be missing.
read.vin.vdsDesc: Positions 4–8: the maker’s own code for model, body, engine and restraints. Only the maker (or a decoder such as NHTSA, for cars sold in the US) can read it, so it cannot be decoded here.
read.vin.plantDesc: Position 11: the factory that built the car. The codes are the maker’s own, so this page cannot name the plant.
read.vin.checkFail: This VIN fails the check. Either a character is mistyped, or it is a European or Asian VIN: only North American cars must pass it.
read.vin.anatomyNote: Read from the VIN alone: maker and country come from the first three characters, the model year from the tenth. Model, engine and trim need a decoder.
read.vin.yearsIntro: The 10th character is the model year. Codes for the current 30-year cycle:
read.vin.yearsNever: The letters I, O, Q, U and Z and the digit 0 are never used as a year code.
read.vin.yearsCycle: The codes repeat every 30 years: A was also 1980. For a car you are looking at, the newer year is almost always the right one; in North America a letter in the 7th position confirms 2010 or later.
read.vin.yearsModelYear: It is the model year, not the build or registration year. A car can be sold a year before or after its model year.
read.vin.registrySince: The open registry publishes VINs only since 2021, so older records may have a plate and no VIN.
read.vin.registryBody: Some records carry a local body number (for example one starting Y6L) instead of the maker’s VIN. Searching by VIN finds the car under either.
read.vin.registryLimits: Since 2026 some registrations have no plate at all. Those cars can only be found by VIN.

value.us.title: US base price (value from the VIN)
value.us.info:
The VIN decoder (NHTSA) knows the original US list price of this exact trim, in dollars. It is shown because it is a second, independent look at the new price.
MSRP - Manufacturer's Suggested Retail Price: the US sticker price of the base version, before options, destination fee and tax
NHTSA - National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, the US road-safety agency whose free VIN decoder gives this price
When an EU price exists - it is only a cross-check next to the Dutch new price; the EU figures above do not change
When there is no EU price - typical for US-market cars - the estimate is built from this price: the same depreciation curve as for EU cars, a wider range, then Ukrainian customs
Not every VIN has a price - many have none, then this block is hidden
value.us.baseInfo: MSRP stands for Manufacturer's Suggested Retail Price: the US list (sticker) price of this trim from the NHTSA VIN decoder (National Highway Traffic Safety Administration), converted at the NBU rate of the day. It excludes options, destination fee and sales tax, and is for a US-spec car.
value.us.euNewInfo: Median Dutch new list price of this model and year without 21 % VAT (value added tax) and BPM (the Dutch car registration tax), so it is comparable to a US price, which has no such taxes.
value.us.gapInfo: How much more (+) or less (-) the US trim costs than the Dutch median. A small gap means the two sources agree; a large one usually means a different engine, trim or equipment.
value.us.valueInfo: The US price after {{age}} years: it keeps about {{percent}} % on the assumed depreciation curve (the Dutch BPM schedule, our assumption for US cars). The range is ±{{spread}} %, wider than for EU cars.
value.us.warnNoEu: No EU price for this model, so the estimate rests on the US list price only. It is rougher than an EU-based one.
value.us.warnDiffers: The US and EU prices differ a lot: the US car may have a different engine, trim or equipment.
value.us.warnTrim: The US price is for the base version of this trim, options are not included. Not a market price.
value.us.altValueInfo: The US base price aged on the same curve ({{age}} years, about {{percent}} % kept, ±{{spread}} %), before Ukrainian customs. Compare it with the EU estimate above: if they are close, the figure is more trustworthy. Not shown as a gap because the Dutch price has VAT and BPM inside.
